facts.text: On this date in 1814, British forces burned Washington D.C. — the only time since 1812 that a foreign power has captured and occupied the U.S. capital.
On August 24, 79 AD, Vesuvius buried Pompeii. The city remained lost for 1,700 years, rediscovered not by archaeologists but by workers digging an aqueduct in 1599.
More people live inside a circle drawn 4,000 km around Bangladesh than outside it — roughly half of all humanity fits within that single boundary.
Canada has more lakes than every other country on Earth combined, containing about 20% of the world's fresh surface water, yet ranks 38th by population.
The country with the highest median age is Monaco at 57 — meaning half its residents are retirees, making it less a nation-state than a luxury retirement community with a flag.

On this day in 1857, the Ohio Life Insurance and Trust Company collapsed, triggering the first worldwide financial crisis — a panic that wiped out American railroad stocks and spread ruin from New York to London within weeks.

On August 24, 1992, Hurricane Andrew made landfall and ultimately caused $15.5 billion in insured losses, bankrupting eleven insurers and permanently reshaping how the industry prices catastrophe risk.
The New York Stock Exchange was founded in 1792 under a buttonwood tree, with 24 brokers agreeing to charge each other fixed commissions — a cartel that survived, largely intact, for 205 years.
Saudi Aramco briefly held a $2.46 trillion market cap in 2022, making it worth more than the entire GDP of France — a single company larger than most nations.

The Dutch East India Company, history's first publicly traded corporation, paid an average annual dividend of 18% for nearly 200 years, a streak no modern blue chip has come remotely close to matching.
On this date in 1989, Voyager 2 flew within 4,950 km of Neptune — the only spacecraft ever to visit the planet, and it did so in a single pass, never to return.
On this date in 2006, the IAU stripped Pluto of its planethood. The vote was cast by just 424 astronomers — roughly 4% of the IAU's membership.
Your body contains roughly 37 trillion cells, but only 1 in 10 of them is human. The rest are bacteria, fungi, and archaea that outnumber you in your own skin.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh approximately 10 million tons on Earth.
Quantum entanglement allows two particles to share a state such that measuring one instantly determines the other — across any distance, with no signal traveling between them.
On this day in 79 AD, Vesuvius buried Pompeii. The city lay undiscovered for 1,700 years — longer than it had existed.
Fax machines were patented in 1843, 33 years before the telephone. Alexander Bain invented a working telegraph-based fax while Bell was still unborn.
On this day in 1991, Linus Torvalds announced Linux to the world. That hobbyist post now underpins 96% of the world's top servers.
The woolly mammoth was still alive when the Great Pyramid was already 1,000 years old. Extinction and antiquity are rarely where we place them.
Nintendo was founded in 1889, making it older than the Eiffel Tower. It spent its first 90 years selling playing cards before touching a single video game.
Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, 2012. Already feels ancient.
Hiraeth (n.): a Welsh longing for a home you cannot return to — or never had. Untranslatable, yet instantly recognizable. No English word has ever filled the gap.
On this day in 1572, the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre began in Paris. The French word 'tocsin' — an alarm bell — entered common use partly through accounts of that night's church bells.
Petrichor (n.): the smell of rain on dry earth. Named in 1964 by Australian scientists Isabel Joy Bear and R.G. Thomas, from Greek petra (stone) and ichor (the fluid in the veins of gods).
On this day in 79 AD, Vesuvius buried Pompeii. The Latin word 'deflagratio' — total destruction by fire — was used by Pliny the Younger in the only eyewitness account of the eruption to survive.

On this date in 2012, Coinbase officially launched to the public, processing its first retail Bitcoin purchases through a simple buy/sell interface that no major exchange had offered before — it handled $1M in monthly volume within weeks.

On this date in 2015, Ethereum's Frontier mainnet had been live for exactly 25 days, with miners earning 5 ETH per block at a time when the network processed fewer daily transactions than a single mid-sized Visa merchant does today.

Bitcoin's UTXO model means your wallet balance doesn't exist — what exists are discrete unspent outputs from prior transactions, each with its own spending conditions, assembled on the fly when you send funds.

The DAO hack of 2016 didn't exploit Ethereum's consensus layer; it exploited a reentrancy bug in Solidity code, draining 3.6M ETH by repeatedly calling the withdrawal function before balances updated.

Satoshi's genesis block coinbase contains the text 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' — both a timestamp and an explicit indictment of the system Bitcoin was designed to replace.
On this date in 2012, Alex Krizhevsky submitted AlexNet to the ImageNet competition. Its 10.8-point error gap over second place was so large that reviewers assumed a reporting mistake.
Today in 2006, Geoffrey Hinton posted the paper that revived deep learning by showing RBMs could pre-train deep networks. The field had been commercially dormant for over a decade.
GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed more electricity than 10,000 US homes use in a year — yet it fits its full context window in less time than it takes to blink.
The first neural network to beat a human champion at Go, AlphaGo, was retired after 3 years. Its successor AlphaZero learned to surpass it from scratch in 8 hours using only self-play.
Transformers now underpin essentially every frontier language model, yet the architecture was invented for machine translation and its authors named the paper after a Michael Bay film.
